newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh's Ershad drops lover to save party.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh's Ershad drops lover to save party.

text.p: Bangladesh's former president Hossain Mohammad Ershad on Friday expelled his long-time lover from his Jatiya Party in a bid to avert a split in the party and save his career.
"He (Ershad) has expelled Zinat Hossain (his lover) from the party," one of Ershad's personal staff told reporters.
Zinat was not available for comment.
Ershad's move came as Bangladesh's third-biggest political party appeared on the verge of a split over his 14-year love affair and his policy differences with other leaders.
The lines were drawn after three key party leaders served Ershad a notice at about midnight on Thursday to "quit the party and transfer the party's leadership" to them.
The rift in the Jatiya party surfaced in March when Ershad expelled former prime minister Kazi Zafar Ahmed from the party after he had criticised the government's policies towards India.
Things appeared to unravel again this week when Ershad said in a newspaper interview that he had proposed to marry Zinat, a fellow Jatiya leader and legislator, after their long relationship.
Ershad had earlier triggered a family dispute by celebrating his birthday with Zinat, wife of former industry secretary Mosharraf Hossain, instead of his wife of more than 40 years, Begum Roushan.

Ershad had "turned the party into his own property and indulged in activities that not only tarnished his personal image but disturbed the party's rank and file", the rebels said in a statement they sent to newspapers late on Thursday.
The rebels, including former prime ministers Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury and Kazi Zafar Ahmed and former deputy premier Shah Moazzem Hossain, said they had conveyed their views to Ershad.
They said a replacement for the former military ruler released from jail three months ago will be chosen in a party caucus the rebels plan to hold in May.
Under tremendous pressure from the party and his relatives, Ershad moved to pacify his followers on Wednesday night, saying "politics (not Zinat) is my first love".
And in a surprise move on Thursday, the 68-year-old former army lieutenant-general said he had severed his relations with Zinat and asked her to refrain from all Jatiya Party activities.
Ershad, who seized power in a bloodless coup in 1982, was deposed in an opposition-led people's uprising in 1990, and was sent to jail. He was freed in January.
Kazi Zafar Ahmed on Friday dismissed Ershad's decision to give up on Zinat, saying "he shouldn't be believed".
Ahmed said the split of the Jatiya Party was inevitable. "We want his (Ershad's) resignation, want to save the party from sex scandal and to play a strong role in opposition," he said.
The rebel leaders earlier said Ershad's personal line of thinking had prevented the party, which has 33 seats in the country's 330-member parliament, playing an effective role.
"Rather it (Jatiya) has become a tool in the hands of the ruling Awami League," one Jatiya leader said.
The Jatiya Party extended its support to the Awami League of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to form a government after general elections last June.
Hasina appointed Jatiya's secretary-general Anwar Hossain Manju as her communications minister, a move she said was an effort to create a government of consensus.
The opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), headed by former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia, described Manju's appointment as a "pay-back" for Jatiya's support.
The rebel Jatiya leaders have also demanded Manju resign from his ministerial job if he wished to stay in the party.
Ershad has often said he did not believe in "opposition for opposition's sake", and that he would support the government for good work and oppose it for bad.
Analysts said say Hasina's government would not fall without the support of the Jatiya party, but the opposition BNP would be put in an advantageous position.
